title: Bioinformatics Module | Bioinformatics and Drug Design
text:
General InformationTP Classes OverviewWeekly Schedule


This 9-week module introduces bioinformatics concepts and tools relevant for pharmaceutical sciences. Students will gain hands-on experience with public databases and online tools to retrieve, analyse, and interpret molecular databases.
Format:

Weekly: 1-hour theory class + 1.5-hour practical class (repeated for 2 student groups).

Target audience: Pharmacy students with introductory knowledge in molecular biology and genetics.
Evaluation:


Participation in class is welcome, and will be positively evaluated.


The details related to the final evaluation format will be discussed and agreed with the students. Either:


A final written exam; or
A video (3 minutes maximum; in groups of 5 students) + oral presentation (10 min) of one drug target (explored in at least 3 of the molecular databases covered in class).









Goal
Learn to independently explore and critically interpret bioinformatics resources in order to connect drugs with their molecular targets and understand their pharmacological, mechanistic, and clinical relevance.


Learning outcomes
By the end of the TP practical classes, students should be able to:

Identify the molecular target(s) of a given drug using authoritative online bioinformatics resources.
Retrieve and interpret relevant molecular information on drug classes, mechanisms of action, target function, 3D structure, and clinical associations.
Integrate data from multiple sources to explain the pharmacological and clinical importance of a drug–target pair.
Demonstrate independent inquiry skills by selecting appropriate databases, justifying search strategies, and reflecting on findings.
Communicate discoveries clearly through concise answers.



TP Activities overview
The students will have access to a hands-on guided tutorial to learn how to explore online resources in order to uncover information that is central to pharmaceutical sciences students.
The following databases will be covered:

Ensembl = gene identity, functional details, and Genome browsing
UniProt = protein details
PDB = protein structure
Drug bank = drug details
ClinPGx = clinical pharmacogenomics
Opentargets = therapeutic drug targets

title: One structure along the RCSB PDB page
section: 1 Why is the PDB relevant for pharmaceutical sciences?
text:
1 Why is the PDB relevant for pharmaceutical sciences?
In the UniProt tutorial you learned what a protein is and what it does. The Protein Data Bank (PDB) shows you what it looks like, atom by atom, often with a drug sitting in its binding pocket.
That view is the foundation of structure-based drug design: once you can see the pocket, you can explain why a drug binds, why a mutation causes resistance, or why a molecule hits one target but not a closely related one. Many modern drugs, such as the HIV protease inhibitors and many kinase inhibitors, were designed or optimised with the help of PDB structures. And structures of COX-2, the enzyme in this tutorial, explained why “coxib” drugs can block COX-2 while sparing COX-1.
The PDB is a single worldwide archive run by the wwPDB partners. RCSB PDB (USA) is one of its portals; PDBe (Europe) and PDBj (Japan) serve the same data with different tools. The archive holds structures solved experimentally (X-ray crystallography, cryo-electron microscopy, NMR), and RCSB also displays computed models (for example from AlphaFold), clearly labelled as such.

title: One structure along the RCSB PDB page
text:
2 About this tutorial
Aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) block the cyclooxygenase enzymes, COX-1 and COX-2, which start the production of prostaglandins (the local messengers behind pain, fever and inflammation). Aspirin is unusual: it does not just sit in the enzyme, it transfers an acetyl group onto a serine in the active site (Ser-530) and then leaves as salicylate.
The PDB entry used shows human COX-2 with salicylate bound. Its UniProt protein is Human Prostaglandin G/H synthase 2 (the UniProt page complements the information on PDB, so it is useful to have both pages open side by side.






NoteBackground reading






PDB-101 Molecule of the Month on Cyclooxygenase (D. Goodsell, 2001): a short, beautifully illustrated introduction to aspirin’s target.
The RCSB Guide to understanding PDB data: short pages on resolution, R-values, biological assemblies and more.

title: One structure along the RCSB PDB page
text:
3 Finding the right entry
The search bar sits at the top of every RCSB page. Like UniProt, it accepts free text, but it also accepts identifiers from other databases.






Tip🔬 Hands on: a broad search




Open https://www.rcsb.org.
Type cyclooxygenase-2 in the search bar and run the search (click the magnifying glass icon or hit enter).
Look at the left-hand panel of the results page (the refinements).









Warning❓ Question




How many structures come back? Write the number down.
Which categories can you use to narrow the list on the left-hand side?







NoteShow answer






184 structures are matched by this query (the exact number grows every week). Too many to browse by hand, and they include COX-2 from several species and with many different inhibitors.
Among others: Organism, Experimental Method, Refinement Resolution, Release Date, Protein modifications, and more. Refinements are the quickest way to cut a large result set down to what you need.






As with UniProt, a unique identifier is a much sharper tool than free text.






Tip🔬 Hands on: search by UniProt accession and refine




Search for Human Prostaglandin G/H synthase 2 in UniProt.
Select the entry from PTGS2 gene. Note the UniProt id number.
In RCSB PDB search with the UniProt accession number.
In the refinements, tick Experimental Method: X-RAY DIFFRACTION.
Sort the results in the right-hand box by Resolution (best to worst).









Warning❓ Question




What is the UniProt accession of human COX-2?
Why does searching by UniProt accession give a cleaner list than cyclooxygenase-2?
Find 5F1A in the list (or simply type 5F1A in the search bar). What happens when you search for an exact PDB ID?







NoteShow answer






P35354
The accession points to exactly one protein from one organism. Every hit is human COX-2, whereas the free text also matches mouse COX-2, COX-1, and papers that merely mention the name.
You land directly on the Structure Summary page of that entry. A PDB ID is unique, so there is nothing to choose between.












NotePDB IDs are getting longer



Classic PDB IDs have four characters (a digit plus three letters or digits). Because the archive is running out of combinations, the wwPDB is introducing extended IDs. The page header already shows both forms: 5F1A and pdb_00005f1a. They refer to the same entry.

title: One structure along the RCSB PDB page
text:
4 Reading the Structure Summary page






Tip🔬 Hands on: open the entry



Go to https://www.rcsb.org/structure/5F1A.








Figure 1: Biological assembly of 5F1A: two copies of COX-2 forming a dimer. Image from RCSB PDB.



Along the top there is a row of tabs:

Structure Summary
Structure
Annotations
Experiment
Sequence
Genome
Ligands
Versions

On the right, the Download Files menu gives you the FASTA sequence, the coordinates files (PDBx/mmCIF or legacy PDB format), the experimental data, and the validation report.
We will start now on the Structure Summary tab and scroll down.

4.1 The ID card
The header tells you, in a few lines, what was studied and how: title, DOI, classification, organism, expression system, mutations, deposition and release dates, and authors.






Warning❓ Question




In which organism was the protein made (expression system)? Why not simply use the bacterial system E. coli? (Hint: look at the Macromolecules section and the sugars listed further down the page.)
How long did it take from deposition to release? Why is there a delay at all?







NoteShow answer






Spodoptera frugiperda, insect cells (the baculovirus system). COX-2 is a eukaryotic, glycosylated, membrane-associated enzyme. Bacteria cannot add sugars (N-glycosylation) and often fail to fold such proteins correctly. Insect cells do both.
Deposited 2015-11-30, released 2016-03-16: about three and a half months. Entries are processed and validated by wwPDB biocurators, and authors can hold release until their paper is published.








4.2 Experimental snapshot: how good is this structure?
Every structure is a model built to explain experimental data. Before you trust it, check two things.

Resolution (in Å) describes the level of detail in the data. Smaller is better: at around 1.5 Å you can see individual atoms; at around 3.5 Å you see the shape of side chains but not their fine detail.
R-values measure how well the model agrees with the data. R-work uses the data the model was built on. R-free uses a small set (around 5%) of data kept aside as a test. Lower is better, and R-free should not be much higher than R-work.







Warning❓ Question




What method was used, and what are the resolution, R-work and R-free?
Look at the coloured wwPDB validation slider. What metrics are shown, and what is their meaning? (Hint: Click the ? icon to obtain more information).







NoteShow answer






X-ray diffraction, 2.38 Å, R-work 0.174, R-free 0.218. This is a good, typical-quality structure: detailed enough to place a small ligand like salicylate, and the gap between R-work and R-free (about 0.04) is normal.
Each bar compares one quality metric (such as R-free, clashscore, Ramachandran outliers and side-chain outliers) with all other X-ray structures in the PDB, and with structures of similar resolution. Markers towards the blue end are better than most; towards the red end, are worse.












Warning❓ Question



Critical thinking question
Use your favourite Large Language Model (LLM) AI chat to ask:
“Explain what R-free is in X-ray crystallography, why it was introduced, and what values indicate a reliable structure. Answer briefly, for postgraduate pharmaceutical sciences students.”
Compare answers with your colleagues. Do they agree on the “good” values? How could you check them? (Hint: the PDB-101 guide has a page on R-values here.






NoteShow answer





R-free is calculated with a random subset of the data (typically 5 to 10%) that is excluded from refinement. Because the model never “saw” those data, R-free cannot be improved by over-fitting, so it is an honest test of the model. As a rough rule, R-free values near or below 0.25 are typical of well-refined structures at medium resolution, and the gap to R-work is usually below about 0.05. Always compare with structures of similar resolution rather than trusting one fixed threshold.







4.3 Literature
Each entry is linked to its primary citation, with its abstract.






Warning❓ Question




Which paper describes this structure, and which other PDB entries were published with it?







NoteShow answer






Lucido et al. (2016) Crystal Structure of Aspirin-Acetylated Human Cyclooxygenase-2: Insight into the Formation of Products with Reversed Stereochemistry. Biochemistry 55: 1226-1238. Related structures: 5F19 (aspirin-acetylated human COX-2) and 5FDQ (a mouse COX-2 mutant, S530T).








4.4 Macromolecules and assembly
The Macromolecules table lists every polymer chain: its name, chains, length, organism, gene and EC number, with links out to UniProt, PHAROS and GTEx. Just above it, the page describes the biological assembly.






NoteAsymmetric unit versus biological assembly



A crystal is built from a small repeating box, the asymmetric unit: what the crystallographer actually modelled. It may contain one copy of the protein, several, or half of a functional complex. The biological assembly is the form believed to exist in the cell. They are not always the same, so check which one you are looking at.








Warning❓ Question




How many protein chains are there, and how many residues long is each?
What is the global stoichiometry and symmetry of the biological assembly?
How many glycosylation sites are annotated?







NoteShow answer






Two chains (A and B) of the same protein, Prostaglandin G/H synthase 2, 553 residues each. Only one residue of the 1,106 deposited is missing from the model.
Homo 2-mer (A2), with cyclic C2 symmetry: COX-2 works as a dimer of two identical subunits (Figure 1).
Two. The sugar chains (N-acetylglucosamine and mannose) appear in the Oligosaccharides section, confirming the protein was glycosylated by the insect cells.








4.5 Small molecules
Now scroll to the Small Molecules table. Each ligand has a short three-character ID (its “chemical component” code), a name, a formula and links to its 3D interactions.




















TipNot every ligand is biology



A structure faithfully records everything in the crystal, including buffers, detergents and cryoprotectants. Before you draw conclusions about a “ligand”, check whether it makes sense biologically, and check the Experiment page (Section 9) for what was in the crystallization drop.

title: One structure along the RCSB PDB page
text:
5 Exploring in 3D with Mol*
The Mol* (MolStar) viewer is built into the RCSB site. You do not need to install anything.






Tip🔬 Hands on: look at the whole protein




Click the Structure tab (or Explore in 3D: Structure under Biological Assembly 1).
Rotate (left-click and drag), zoom (scroll wheel) and move (right-click and drag).
In the right-hand panel, open Components and turn on and off the visibility (eye icon) of the polymer, the ligands, the carbohydrates and the water.
Notice the tool bar on the right side the viewport. Click the Expanded viewport icon (looks like a square) to expand the viewer to full screen. You must leave the expanded viewer to access the panel options again.
Hover over any part of the molecule and read the label at the bottom right: chain, residue name and number.
Explore the viewer window header and its options (select a molecule from the box, and then click on its components to zoom-in to it).
Reload the page to reset the viewing parameters.









Warning❓ Question




How many copies of the ligands salicylate (2-HYDROXYBENZOIC ACID) and cobalt porphyrin (PROTOPORPHYRIN IX CONTAINING CO) can you find, and in which chains? (Hint: In the right-hand panel you can hide from view the molecules that are not ligands). What does that tell you about the active sites?
What secondary structure dominates COX-2: helices or sheets (cartoon arrows)?







NoteShow answer






Two of each: one salicylate and one porphyrin per chain. Each subunit of the dimer carries its own complete set of active sites.
Mainly alpha helices. The small beta-sheet regions belong mostly to the EGF-like domain.






Now zoom in on the drug.






Tip🔬 Hands on: the salicylate binding site




Go back to the Structure Summary tab. In the Small Molecules table, find the SAL row and click Interactions: Focus chain E [auth A].
The view zooms in on salicylate, shows the surrounding residues as sticks, and draws dashed lines for non-covalent interactions (hydrogen bonds, ionic, pi-stacking, hydrophobic).
Hover over the neighbouring residues and over the dashed lines to identify them.
Measure a distance: switch on selection mode (arrow icon on the right of the viewer), click the salicylate hydroxyl oxygen and then the side-chain oxygen (OG) of Ser-499 (they become highlighted in green), and then in the Measurements section of right-hand panel click Add Distances.
Repeat steps 1 to 4 for the salicylate in chain B (Focus chain L [auth B]).









Warning❓ Question




Which residues surround salicylate? Which of them form hydrogen bonds or ionic interactions with it?
What distance did you measure between salicylate and Ser-499, the residue that aspirin acetylates?
Does salicylate bind in the same way in both chains?







NoteShow answer







Salicylate sits inside the long, mostly hydrophobic cyclooxygenase channel, the same channel where the natural substrate, arachidonic acid, binds. Useful landmarks in this channel are Arg-80 and Tyr-324 (the “constriction” near the entrance), Tyr-354 (the catalytic tyrosine) and Ser-499 (aspirin’s acetylation target). Your list of contacts should include residues from this set plus hydrophobic neighbours; the polar interactions involve salicylate’s carboxylate and hydroxyl groups.
Chain A: 6.03 Å. Chain B: 5.67 Å.
The pose is very similar in the two chains (remember that 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ meters). Small differences between chains are common: each copy in the crystal is an independent observation.












Tip🔬 Hands on: is the ligand really there?




Back on the Structure Summary page, click Interactions & Density for SAL (chain E).
The mesh around the atoms is the electron density: the experimental evidence for where the atoms are.
Compare the density around salicylate with the density around a well-ordered residue next to it.









Warning❓ Question



Why is it worth checking the electron density for a ligand, rather than simply trusting its coordinates?






NoteShow answer





The coordinates of a ligand are placed by the crystallographer. If the density does not clearly cover the ligand, its position (or even its presence) may be doubtful. For drug design this matters a lot: a wrongly placed ligand leads to wrong conclusions about which interactions drive binding. The Ligands tab of the entry summarises this with ligand quality scores (fit to density and geometry). More information on this subject will be approached in the Drug modelling module.

title: One structure along the RCSB PDB page
text:
6 The ligand page
Every chemical component in the PDB has its own page.






Tip🔬 Hands on



In the Small Molecules table, click the ligand ID SAL, or go to https://www.rcsb.org/ligand/SAL.








Warning❓ Question




In how many PDB entries is SAL found as a standalone ligand? And covalently linked?
What is its DrugBank ID? What is salicylic acid used for?
Look at the Drug Targets table. Besides Prostaglandin G/H synthase 1 (COX-1) and Prostaglandin G/H synthase 2 (COX-2), which other human proteins are listed? Why could this matter for a patient?







NoteShow answer






73 entries as a standalone ligand and 2 where it is covalently linked (at the time of writing).
DB00936. It is widely used in dermatology (acne, psoriasis, warts, corns), and its salts, the salicylates, are used as analgesics and anti-inflammatories.
Several carbonic anhydrases, an aldo-keto reductase, cytochrome P450 2C9 (as a substrate), albumin, and organic anion transporters (OAT1, OAT3). These are potential off-targets and routes of metabolism and transport: they help explain side effects and drug-drug interactions.












NoteLigand IDs are another universal key



Just as P35354 identifies a protein, SAL identifies a chemical component across the whole archive. From the ligand page you can also run a chemical similarity search to find structures with related molecules: a first step in exploring structure-activity relationships.

title: One structure along the RCSB PDB page
text:
7 Annotations






Tip🔬 Hands on



Click the Annotations tab.


This page gathers what other resources say about the protein chains: structural domain classifications (SCOP2, ECOD, CATH), protein families (Pfam, InterPro), Gene Ontology terms, and disease associations (Pharos).






Warning❓ Question




Which two kinds of domain do CATH and InterPro identify in COX-2?
What is the Pfam family? What does it tell you about COX-2’s evolutionary relatives?
Name three diseases associated with COX-2 in the Pharos section. Why would a drug target be linked to so many diseases?







NoteShow answer






An EGF-like (laminin-type) domain, and a large haem peroxidase domain (animal type), which holds both the peroxidase and cyclooxygenase active sites.
PF03098, Animal haem peroxidase. COX-2 belongs to the same family as enzymes like myeloperoxidase (SCOP2 calls it Myeloperoxidase-like): its peroxidase function is ancient; the cyclooxygenase activity is its specialisation.
For example rheumatoid arthritis, colorectal cancer, familial adenomatous polyposis, gastric ulcer, cardiovascular disease. Prostaglandins act in almost every tissue, so COX-2 is involved in inflammation, cancer, the cardiovascular system and more. This is also why COX inhibitors have both wide uses and wide side effects.

title: One structure along the RCSB PDB page
text:
8 Sequence and Genome






Tip🔬 Hands on




Click the Sequence tab. Look at the tracks aligned along the sequence of chain A: the UniProt sequence, the modelled regions, secondary structure, domains and binding sites.
Click the Explore Sequence Annotations in 3D link on top of the sequence viewer and highlight, for example, the secondary structure domains to see their 3D location compared to their 2D linear sequence.
Then click the Genome tab.









Warning❓ Question




The crystallized chain is 553 residues long. How long is the full human COX-2 in UniProt (P35354)? Which parts are missing, and why might that be? (Hint: In the Feature viewer tab of UniProt explore the PDBe coverage and the Molecule processing tracks to check which regions are not solved in 3D).
On which chromosome is the PTGS2 gene located?







NoteShow answer






604 residues. The N-terminal signal peptide (cleaved off naturally when the protein enters the endoplasmic reticulum) is not part of the crystallized chain, and the chain stops before the flexible C-terminal tail. Flexible, disordered regions are often removed or simply not visible in crystal structures: a structure rarely shows the whole protein.
Chromosome 1 (1q31). The Genome view maps the protein back onto its gene, exons and transcripts, connecting to what you did in the Ensembl tutorials.

title: One structure along the RCSB PDB page
text:
9 Experiment and validation






Tip🔬 Hands on




Click the Experiment tab. Observe the rich standardized description of the experimental settings used to obtain this data record.
From the Structure Summary page, open the Full Report (wwPDB validation report, PDF). This is the document that sustains this database entry.



The Experiment tab records how the structure was obtained, from crystal to final model. You do not need to understand every number, but three points are worth noticing for 5F1A.
Crystallization. The protein was crystallized by sitting-drop vapour diffusion at pH 7.5 and 23 °C (296 K). The solution contained polyacrylic acid, HEPES buffer, magnesium chloride and 0.6% octyl glucoside, a detergent that keeps this membrane-associated protein soluble. This explains two of the “leftover” ligands present in the Small Molecules section: BOG is the octyl glucoside itself, and AKR (acrylic acid) most likely comes from the polyacrylic acid.
Data collection. The diffraction data were collected at a synchrotron (the Advanced Photon Source, beamline 17-ID), at the temperature of 100 K. Crystals are routinely frozen like this to limit damage from the very intense X-ray beam.
Structure solution. The structure was solved by molecular replacement: a previously known, similar COX-2 structure was used as the starting model. For well-studied proteins like COX-2, this is the quickest route to a new structure, for example a new drug complex.

title: One structure along the RCSB PDB page
text:
10 Versions






Tip🔬 Hands on



Click the Versions tab.








Warning❓ Question




How many versions of this entry exist?
Two updates are labelled Remediation. What was fixed in each?
Did the authors’ experimental data change in any of these versions?







NoteShow answer






Seven (version 1.0 in March 2016 up to version 2.2 in August 2026).
Carbohydrate remediation (version 2.0, 2020): the archive-wide re-description of sugar chains. Metalloprotein remediation (version 2.2, 2026): a re-description of metal sites, relevant here because of the cobalt porphyrin.
No. Updates concern annotation, derived calculations, and how the data are represented. As in UniProt, the knowledge around an entry keeps improving, even when the experiment stays the same.

title: One structure along the RCSB PDB page
text:
11 Going further (optional)
If you finish early, try one of these.






Tip🔬 Hands on: before and after aspirin




Navigate to the main page of RCSB PDB, click the All tools button, and select Analysis. Open the Pairwise Structure Alignment tool (click Go to Tool).
Align chain A of 5F1A (salicylate) with chain A of 5F19 (aspirin-acetylated COX-2). Leave the default alignment method, and click Compare.
In 5F19, find Ser-530 and look at its side chain. In 5F1A, compare it with where salicylate sits.

title: One structure along the RCSB PDB page
text:
Key points






TipTake home messages




A PDB entry is an experimental model: always check method, resolution and R-values before trusting details.
Search with identifiers (PDB ID, UniProt accession, ligand ID) rather than free text whenever you can.
The biological assembly may differ from what was modelled in the crystal.
Not every small molecule in a structure is biologically relevant: detergents, buffers and cryoprotectants are recorded too.
Mol* lets you see exactly where a drug binds and which residues it touches; the electron density tells you whether to believe it.
Ligand, annotation, sequence and genome pages connect the structure to DrugBank, UniProt, Pfam, GO and the genome.
The Versions tab shows that even an archived structure keeps being curated.

text:
Overview






NoteQuestions this lesson answers




How can I find information about a gene, its transcripts, and the protein it encodes in Ensembl?

What functions is PCSK9 annotated with? Where did you find this information?

Critical thinking exercise: Does it make sense for a gene to have a function?






NoteShow answer






66 structures.
27 ligands, which you can see by following the PDBe-KB link (Ligands tab). For example:

NAG (2-acetamido-2-deoxy-beta-D-glucopyranose)
FUC (alpha-L-fucopyranose)
… (and others) …

GOA (Glycolic acid)
PG4 (Tetraethylene glycol)

Functional information is available in all three databases (UniProtKB, InterPro, and PDBe-KB):

Crucial player in the regulation of plasma cholesterol homeostasis. Binds to members of the low-density lipoprotein receptor family: low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR), very low-density lipoprotein receptor (VLDLR), apolipoprotein E receptor (LRP1/APOER), and apolipoprotein E receptor 2 (LRP8/APOER2), and promotes their degradation in intracellular acidic compartments.
Acts via a non-proteolytic mechanism to enhance the degradation of the hepatic LDLR through a clathrin LDLRAP1/ARH-mediated pathway.
May prevent the recycling of LDLR from endosomes to the cell surface, or direct it to lysosomes for degradation.
Can induce ubiquitination of LDLR, leading to its subsequent degradation.

Involved in the disposal of non-acetylated intermediates of BACE1 in the early secretory pathway.

Tip🔬 Hands on




In the Transcripts tab, click the diagram of transcript ENST00000302118.5 to see general information about this transcript.

Which diseases are associated with this gene/protein?
Is it a Mendelian disease? What is its mode of inheritance?







NoteShow answer






12 exons in total, all of them reported as coding.
Hypercholesterolemia (familial hypercholesterolemia).
Yes, it is a Mendelian disease with an autosomal dominant (AD) mode of inheritance. This means that inheriting a single altered copy of the gene, from one parent, is enough to cause the condition.








1.4 Export the gene/transcript sequence






Tip🔬 Hands on: export the sequence




In the Feature explorer, click the transcript of interest, and then click the Download arrow.
Notice that when you tick the box next to cDNA, CDS, or any of the other options, the transcript diagram highlights which parts of the sequence will be included in the downloaded file.

Warning❓ Question



What information does the FASTA header contain?






NoteShow answer





A FASTA header is the first line of each sequence entry, and it starts with a > symbol. It describes the sequence that begins on the next line. The header should include a stable and unique identifier for the sequence, and it often includes other details, such as the gene name and the species. For example:
>ENST00000302118.5|PCSK9|Homo_sapiens

How many protein-coding genes are in the region you selected?







NoteShow answer






57227415 bp (57227415 - 1 + 1). Because the region starts at position 1, its size is the same as its end coordinate.
Answers will vary depending on the region you chose. I chose the coordinates Y:1084826-6714927, which contain 10 genes on the forward strand and 7 genes on the reverse strand. I counted them by eye, because the new Ensembl interface does not yet offer tools to summarise the genes in a region.

text:
4 Exploring a genetic variant
The SNP rs1738074 has been reported as a genetic risk factor for several diseases. Now we want to explore in detail what this variant is, and why it might be a genetic risk factor.






Note💡 Remember: what are genetic variants?



A genetic variant is a difference in the DNA sequence between individuals, or between an individual and the reference genome. Variants range in size from a single base (single-nucleotide variants, SNVs; common SNVs are often called SNPs) to small insertions and deletions, up to large structural variants that can delete or duplicate entire genes.
Why do they matter in pharmaceutical sciences?

Drug response (pharmacogenomics): variants in genes that encode drug-metabolising enzymes, such as CYP2D6 or CYP2C19, change how patients respond to a drug, affecting both its efficacy and the risk of adverse reactions.
Drug targets: people who carry natural loss-of-function variants in PCSK9 have low LDL cholesterol and a lower risk of heart disease. This finding helped establish PCSK9 as a drug target.
Diagnosis and treatment choice: some variants increase disease risk, and others, such as those in BRCA2, can guide diagnosis and treatment decisions.









Tip🔬 Hands on: find the variant




Search Ensembl directly for rs1738074.
Open the Genome browser view and inspect the information about this genetic variant.









Note🔎 Want to know more about this variant?



Click the ... (three dots) in the top-right corner of the variant tab, next to the name rs1738074. This gives you access to more information about the variant, including its population genetics data. We will not explore this further in this class, but it is useful to know that the linked dbSNP database provides detailed information on genetic variants, such as their associations with phenotypes and diseases, in case you ever need to explore them further.








Warning❓ Question




In which gene is this single-nucleotide variant (SNV) found?
On which chromosome is the gene located?
In how many transcripts is the variant found?
In which region of the transcript is the variant located?
What are the coordinates of the variant?







NoteShow answer






This SNP is in the TAGAP gene.
This gene is on chromosome 6 (6:159034481-159044991).
It is found in 7 transcripts of TAGAP. It is also located in an intron of one long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) transcript of TAGAP-AS1, on the forward strand.
In the 5’ UTR (5’ untranslated region).
The rs1738074 variant is located at 6:159044945 (chromosome 6, position 159044945, in the GRCh38 assembly).

title: Ensembl genes and transcripts | Part 2
section: 5 VEP analysis of a structural variant
text:
5 VEP analysis of a structural variant
A tumour sample from a patient with breast cancer carries a large genomic deletion, described here in VCF (Variant Call Format):
13  32307062    sv1 .   <DEL>   .   .   SVTYPE=DEL;END=32908738
In plain words, this line describes a deletion (<DEL>) on chromosome 13 that starts at position 32,307,062 and ends at position 32,908,738 (about 600 kb).
We now want to know whether this variant could be relevant to the disease: which genes does it affect, and how? To answer this, we will use the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor (VEP).






Note💡 What is VEP?



VEP is a tool that takes a list of genetic variants (for example, from a patient’s sequencing data) and predicts their effects. For each variant, VEP reports:

the genes and transcripts that it overlaps;
where in the transcript it falls (for example, in an exon, an intron, or a UTR);
its predicted molecular consequence, using standard terms (for example, missense_variant when one amino acid is replaced by another, or transcript_ablation when a whole transcript is deleted).

Why is this important? Sequencing a person’s genome typically reveals millions of variants, and most of them are harmless. VEP is a first step to sort through them and find the few that are likely to affect gene function, and that could therefore help with a diagnosis or a treatment decision. Keep in mind that these are predictions: they must be confirmed by experimental or clinical evidence.








Tip🔬 Hands on: run VEP




Click Ensembl VEP at the top of any Ensembl page.
Read the help page (click the ? sign).
Add the Human genome (click the + sign in the Genome row).
Give the job a descriptive name, for example Patient deletion exercise. Naming jobs is a good habit: the name is how you tell results apart later, and it is what appears in the browser when you view the data.
Click the + sign in the Variants row, and paste the VCF line shown above (use the copy button in the top-right corner of the code block).
Click Add.
Keep the default job options and click Run. By default, the results list the genes and transcripts that each variant falls in, and the predicted molecular consequence for each one.









Warning❓ Question




How many genes are affected?
What are the predicted molecular consequences of this variant?







NoteShow answer






7 genes are affected: N4BP2L2, PDS5B, N4BP2L1, BRCA2, ZAR1L, IFIT1P1, and ATP8A2P2. Notice that BRCA2, a well-known breast cancer susceptibility gene, is among them.
Mostly transcript_ablation, but also coding_sequence_variant, 5_prime_UTR_variant, and intron_variant for the ZAR1L gene.






Critical thinking exercise: Use the AI chatbot Perplexity to learn the meaning of the most common predicted molecular consequence. Ask: “In the context of the Variant Effect Predictor for genomic variant analysis, what does ‘[insert the most common consequence here]’ mean? Explain it using a clear, concise, scientific yet simple tone, for postgraduate students.” As before, check critically whether the answer makes sense.

title: Ensembl genes and transcripts | Part 2
text:
Key points






TipTake-home messages




You can search Ensembl using a gene name, a variant identifier (such as an rs number), or a set of genomic coordinates.
Ensembl links to specialised databases (UniProtKB, InterPro, PDBe-KB, OMIM, and dbSNP) with detailed information on protein function, structure, diseases, and variants.
A gene usually has many transcripts. Choose one deliberately, and prefer the MANE Select transcript when available (a representative transcript agreed on by Ensembl and NCBI).
Genomic coordinates are only meaningful with an assembly version (for example, GRCh38), and alleles are only meaningful with a strand.
VEP predicts the consequences of variants of any size, from single-nucleotide variants to large structural variants, and helps you find the ones most likely to matter.
AI tools can help you learn, but always check their answers critically.

title: One protein along the UniProt page
section: 1 Why is UniProt relevant for pharmaceutical sciences?
text:
1 Why is UniProt relevant for pharmaceutical sciences?
Almost every drug works by acting on a protein, and UniProt is the central, trusted reference where you can find what that protein is, what it does, where it’s found, how it varies between people and species, and which other resources (structures, drugs, pathways) are linked to it.
Whatever direction your pharmaceutical career takes, you’ll regularly need a reliable answer to “what is this protein and why does it matter for this drug?”, and UniProt is where that answer lives.

title: One protein along the UniProt page
text:
2 About this lesson
This lesson uses human opsins as a worked example. Opsins sit in the cells of the retina, where they capture light and start the signalling cascade that produces vision. When they are disrupted, the result can be colour blindness or other visual impairment.
Almost all of the work happens on the UniProt website.






NoteSources and further reading





The original Galaxy Training Network lesson drew on the UniProt help page Explore UniProtKB entry, and chose the topic following Gale Rhodes’ Bioinformatics Tutorial. The latter can no longer be followed step by step (the resources have changed too much) but is still a good source of background on opsins and on building structural models from evolutionary information.

title: One protein along the UniProt page
text:
3 Finding the right entry
The starting point for protein annotation is UniProtKB. You can query it with free text, a gene name, or a protein name. Let us begin with something deliberately vague.






Tip🔬 Hands on: a broad search




Open https://www.uniprot.org/.
Type Human opsin into the search bar.
Run the search.









Warning❓ Question



How many results come back?






NoteShow answer





Around 524 (at the time of creating this tutorial). Far too many to inspect by hand, even though (spoiler alert) the entry we want is near the top.





Free text is too “vague”. A better strategy is to search on a unique identifier. The gene we are interested in called OPN1LW.






Tip🔬 Hands on: search by gene name




Type OPN1LW into the search bar.
Run the search.









Warning❓ Question




How many results now?
What is still missing from the query that could focus our search? (Hint: Think about the organism of interest.)







NoteShow answer






Over 240 results (at the time of creating this tutorial).
Human is our organism of interest. The same gene name is used across many species, so by adding Human to the query, we restrict the search.












Tip🔬 Hands on: search by gene name plus organism




Type Human OPN1LW into the search bar.
Run the search.









Warning❓ Question




How many results now?
Is there a hit whose gene name is exactly OPN1LW?







NoteShow answer






8 results! (at the time of creating this tutorial).
Yes, the first hit carries the label Gene: OPN1LW, RCP.






That first hit, P04000 (OPSR_HUMAN), is our target. Three things are worth noticing before opening it:

The protein name (OPSR_HUMAN) and the gene name (OPN1LW) are different, and so are their identifiers. Gene and protein are distinct entities with distinct names.
The entry carries a gold star, meaning it has been manually annotated and curated by a human (Swiss-Prot) rather than generated automatically (via TrEMBL).
The annotation score is 5/5, meaning that its annotation is detailed and rich.

title: One protein along the UniProt page
text:
4 Reading the entry page






Tip🔬 Hands on: open the entry



Click on P04000 · OPSR_HUMAN, or go directly to https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P04000/entry.








Figure 1: The header of a UniProt entry page.



The page is long, so the left-hand navigation bar does a lot of work. It stays fixed as you scroll, and just reading it tells you what the database holds about this entry:



known functions
taxonomy
subcellular location
variants and associated diseases
post-translational modifications (PTMs)
expression




interactions
structure
domains and their classification
sequences
similar proteins
homologs



At the very top of the page you get the “ID card” of the protein:



accession number and entry name
the protein and gene names
whether the entry has been reviewed by a curator (Status)
the organism




protein length (number of amino acids)
the evidence level for the protein’s existence
and the annotation score (how well is the database entry annotated)



Below the header there are 7 tabs: Entry, Variant viewer, Feature viewer, Genomic coordinates, Publications, External links, and History.
Notice that just above the tabs is a toolbar: From the Tools you can BLAST the sequence, add the entry to a basket for later analysis, or Download it.
For now, we will continue on the Entry tab.

4.1 Function
The Function section opens with a short free-text summary: visual pigments are the light-absorbing molecules behind vision, and consist of an apoprotein (opsin) covalently bound to cis-retinal.
Two sentences to summarize decades of research. That compression is possible because someone has already done the curation work, and because the protein has been classified in the Gene Ontology (GO), which describes molecular function, biological process, and cellular component.
GO is a good example of a resource that flattens a very complex body of knowledge into a graph. Detail is lost, but in exchange the information becomes countable, comparable, and machine-readable, which is exactly what makes summary pages like this one possible.






Warning❓ Question




Which GO terms is this protein annotated with, for:


molecular function?
biological process?


Explore the GO-CAM models tab. What information does it provide? (Hint: Use the green HELP button on the right side to deepen your knowledge.)







NoteShow answer






GO annotation:


Molecular Function: G protein-coupled receptor, Photoreceptor protein, Receptor, Retinal protein, Transducer.
Biological Process: Sensory transduction, Vision.


This proteins is part of the “Red light signaling mediated by OPN1LW photoreceptor via G-alpha-t(transducin)_Visual perception” model. It interacts directly or indirectly with 6 other genes, and requires Calcium and Sodium ions.








4.2 Names and taxonomy
The next section holds more structured information, including the taxonomic placement of the protein. It also lists other identifiers that point at the same biological entity, or at linked entities (for example associated diseases under MIM).






Warning❓ Question




What is the taxonomic identifier of the organisms that presents this protein?
What is the proteome identifier?







NoteShow answer






9606, that is Homo sapiens.
UP000005640, and this protein is a component of chromosome X.








4.3 Subcellular location
We already know where the protein is in the body (the retina). But, where is it in the cell?






Warning❓ Question




Where does UniProt place this protein within the cell?
Is that consistent with the description in the GO Annotation tab?







NoteShow answer






It is described by UniProt as a multi-pass membrane protein: it is embedded in the membrane and crosses it several times.
Yes. GO is more specific, naming the cone photoreceptor disc membrane.






This section also has a Features area showing which portions of the sequence sit inside the membrane (transmembrane) and which do not (topological domain).






Warning❓ Question



How many transmembrane and topological domains are listed?






NoteShow answer





7 transmembrane regions and 8 topological domains.







4.4 Disease and variants
This gene and protein are linked to several diseases. The section describes those associations and lists the specific variants implicated in each.






Warning❓ Question



Critical thinking question
Use your favorite Large Language Model (LMM) AI chat to ask the following question:
“In the context of studying the effects of genetic variants, what types of study establish that a genetic variant is associated with a disease? Answer in brief, clear, and scientific tone for postgraduate pharmaceutical sciences students.”
Compare your answer with the answers of your colleagues: Is it correct? Is it complete? Does it match your knowledge? How do you validate the answer?






NoteShow answer





There are, at least, 3 common study designs:

Genome-wide association studies (GWAS). Scan whole genomes across large cohorts to find common variants that track with a trait or disease.
Case-control studies. Compare the frequency of specific variants between affected and unaffected individuals.
Family studies. Follow inheritance patterns within families in which several members are affected, which can pinpoint candidate genes.






A Features area maps the natural variants along the sequence, and points you to the more detailed view in the Variant viewer app. Do not click on it yet! Resist the temptation for now.


4.5 PTM and processing
A post-translational modification (PTM) is a covalent event after translation: either a proteolytic cleavage, or the addition of a chemical group to an amino acid (e.g. glycosylation adds sugar, lipidation adds fats).






Warning❓ Question




Which post-translational modifications are annotated here?
What is the meaning of these modifications? (Hint: Click the i next to the title PTM/Processing to see a table of the possible PTMs.)







NoteShow answer






Chain, glycosylation, disulfide bond, and modified residue.
These PTMs mean:


Chain: Extent of a polypeptide chain in the mature protein.
Glycosylation: Covalently attached glycan group(s).
Disulfide bond: Cysteine residues participating in disulfide bonds.
Modified residue: Modified residues excluding lipids, glycans and protein crosslinks.








4.6 Expression
For human proteins there is often tissue-level expression information, drawn from resources such as the Expression Atlas.






Warning❓ Question



In which tissue is this protein found?






NoteShow answer





The three colour pigments are found in the cone photoreceptor cells.







4.7 Interaction
Proteins do their work by interacting with their surroundings, and above all with other proteins. This section lists known interactors in a table you can filter by subcellular location, disease, and interaction type. Much of the underlying data comes from databases such as STRING, which is linked directly.






Tip🔬 Hands on: follow the link out to STRING




Click on the STRING link for this protein, and open it in a new tab. Note how many proteins the default network has.
Add more proteins to the network by clicking a few times on the + More button.
In the Clusters tab select k-means clustering, ask for 4 clusters and hit Apply.
Now test the other clustering options. Note the functions of the clusters found.









Warning❓ Question




How many proteins does the default network contain?
What are the overall functions of the 4 clusters obtained by k-means?
How many clusters does the MCL algorithm find, and what are their functions?
How many clusters does the Leiden algorithm find, and what are their functions?







NoteShow answer






11 proteins
Signalling, Light detection, retina proteins, and Tex28 (single protein).
1 cluster related to signalling.
2 clusters related to signalling and light sensing.








4.8 Structure
The Structure section is the way into the three-dimensional world. It reports experimentally determined structures where they exist, and gives you an interactive viewer embedded in the page, so you can rotate the molecule and explore domains, binding sites, and other functional regions without leaving UniProt.






Tip🔬 Hands on: Explore the 3D structure of the protein




Rotate the protein in the viewer. Zoom in and out with the mouse wheel.
Notice the different colors and cartoon shapes (helices, and sheets).
Explore the different models from PDB, AlphaFoldDB, and Others.
Notice just below the title Structure, the banner “View UniProt features on this structure in the Feature Viewer.” Click and open it in a new tab.
Click on Variants, and select only Likely pathogenic or pathogenic.
Click on any variant and notice that the 3D structure below highlights the location of the variant.
Now select only the UniProt reviewed variants.









Warning❓ Question




How many variants are Likely pathogenic and UniProt reviewed?
What diseases are associated with the previous variants?
Can you propose why might amino acid substitutions be disruptive to the protein structure?
How do you explain that different variants located in different places of the protein result in the same disease?







NoteShow answer






3 variants.
The disease associated with each variant is:


Variant 203: C>R (C203R); Disease association: Blue cone monochromacy (BCM).
Variant 307: P>L (P307L); Disease association: Blue cone monochromacy (BCM).
Variant 338: G>E (G338E); Disease association: Colorblindness, partial, protan series (CBP).


Each amino acid has a specific size, charge, polarity, and flexibility that contribute to how the protein folds and holds its 3D shape. When one is replaced by an amino acid with very different properties (for example, a small residue by a bulky one, or a neutral residue by a charged one), it can break important bonds or interactions, distort helices or binding pockets, and prevent the protein from folding correctly, which in turn impacts its function.
A protein’s function depends on its overall 3D structure, not on a single residue. Different mutations can damage different parts of the protein (folding, the retinal pocket, signalling regions), but they all converge on the same outcome: the red opsin is missing or cannot respond properly to light. The disease reflects this shared loss of function, while the severity can vary.








4.9 Family and domains
Going back to the Entry tab, the Family and Domains section places the protein in its evolutionary context: the families, superfamilies, and domains it belongs to, plus conserved regions, motifs, and other notable sequence features.
The Features area confirms that at least one of the two protruding domains (the N-terminal one) is disordered, and reiterates that we are dealing with a transmembrane protein.
The links out to phylogenetic and domain databases are the route into questions of common ancestry and functional specialisation.


4.10 Sequence
Everything above is ultimately encoded in the amino acid sequence. Here you can download the FASTA file, trace the data back to the sequencing experiments that produced it, and see any protein isoforms that have been detected.






Warning❓ Question



How many potential isoforms map to this entry? How long are they?






NoteShow answer





One potential isoform: H0Y622, which is 164 amino acids long.







4.11 Similar proteins and Homologs
The final two sections of the Entry tab lists similar proteins produced by clustering at 100%, 90%, and 50% identity thresholds, and the Homologs section provides orthology and paralogy information which has been retrieved from the Alliance of Genome Resources (AGR).
Recall
Orthology describes genes from different species that have evolved from a common ancestral gene through a speciation event, meaning these genes typically perform similar functions across species.
Paralogy, refers to genes within the same species that originated from duplication events, often resulting in genes with related but distinct functions.






Warning❓ Question




How many similar proteins are there at each threshold: 100%, 90% and 50% similarity?
How many genes are classified as paralogous to OPN1LW?







NoteShow answer






Similar protein numbers:


Cluster membership


Identity threshold
Similar proteins




100%
0


90%
101


50%
516




11 paralogous genes in human.







A pattern should be emerging: much of what we do with protein data is mapping different layers of information onto the same sequence and asking how they relate. The next two tabs do exactly that, visually.

text:
5 Variant viewer






Tip🔬 Hands on



Click the Variant viewer tab on top.


This view maps every known alternative version of the sequence. Some have a known effect (pathogenic or benign); many do not.






Warning❓ Question




How many variants create a stop codon (*) (keeping all consequences and all provenances)?
Is their effect relevant for disease (pathogenic)? Can you propose a reason why?







NoteShow answer






6 variants create a stop (*).
3 are likely pathogenic (half of teh total variants). Stop codon variants can be pathogenic because they may cause premature termination of translation, producing a shortened, nonfunctional protein or triggering degradation of its mRNA through nonsense-mediated decay (NMD). Less commonly, loss of the normal stop codon causes excessive protein extension, which can also disrupt function.






The sheer number of variants is a useful corrective. A “protein sequence” (like a gene sequence, or a structure) is much less of a fixed object than the singular canonical entry suggests.

6 Feature viewer






Tip🔬 Hands on



Click the Feature viewer tab.


The Feature viewer merges all the Features areas scattered through the Entry page into one track-based display: domains and sites, molecule processing, PTMs, topology, proteomics, and variants. Clicking a feature highlights the corresponding region in the structure.






Tip🔬 Hands on: locate the variant in context




Expand the Variants track.
Zoom out.
Click the blue point at position 2.









Warning❓ Question




What is the topology and the domain at position 2?
Which positions of the protein present Post Translational Modifications (PTMs)?







NoteShow answer






Position 2 has an extracelular topology, and it falls in a disordered domain.
CARBOHYD 22-22; CARBOHYD 34-34; DISULFID 126-203; MOD_RES 312-312.

7 Publications






Tip🔬 Hands on



Click the Publications tab.


This tab lists papers relevant to the protein, combining a manually curated list (from UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot) with automatically imported references.
On the left side you can filter by source, by the category of data a paper contributes (function, interaction, sequence, and so on), and by study size (small scale versus large scale).






Warning❓ Question




How many publications are linked to this protein? (Hint: Sum all the sources.)
How many of them contribute information about its function?







NoteShow answer






63 (at the time of creating this tutorial).
30 (at the time of creating this tutorial).

8 External links






Tip🔬 Hands on



Click the External links tab.


This tab gathers every cross-reference scattered across the Entry into one place. The link text usually shows the identifier that represents the same entity in the other database, which is what makes automated cross-referencing possible at all.
For a sense of how tangled that web is, look at the bioDBnet network diagram. Databases are the major nodes, identifiers the minor ones, and the region around the UniProt entry name, Gene ID, and Ensembl Gene ID is extremely dense. The diagram is already partly out of date, which rather makes the point.

9 History






Tip🔬 Hands on



Click the History tab.


The History tab exposes every previous version of the entry’s annotation, in this case going back to 1988, and lets you download them. It is a record of how knowledge about this protein has accumulated and been revised.






Warning❓ Question



How many versions of this entry have there been?






NoteShow answer





Since its first release in 01 November 1988 (38 years ago), this protein has had 219 versions (in October 2026)!

TipTake home messages




UniProtKB entries collect function, taxonomy, localisation, interactions, 3D structure, homology and much more in one curated place.

title: One drug along the DrugBank page
section: 1 Why is DrugBank relevant for pharmaceutical sciences?
text:
1 Why is DrugBank relevant for pharmaceutical sciences?
In the UniProt session you started from a protein. Today you start from the molecule that acts on it.
DrugBank gathers in one entry what a pharmacist or drug developer needs to know about a drug: its chemistry, what it binds, how the body absorbs, transforms and eliminates it, what it interacts with, and how it is marketed. Each piece links to other databases (UniProt, PubChem, ChEMBL, the PDB) through shared identifiers.

title: One drug along the DrugBank page
text:
2 About this lesson
This lesson uses atorvastatin (Lipitor) as a worked example. Atorvastatin is a statin: it lowers blood cholesterol and reduces the risk of heart attack and stroke. For many years it was the best-selling medicine in the world, and it is still one of the most prescribed.

title: One drug along the DrugBank page
text:
3 Finding the entry






Tip🔬 Hands on: find atorvastatin




Open https://go.drugbank.com and log in.
Search for atorvastatin and open the first hit (or go directly to https://go.drugbank.com/drugs/DB01076).









Warning❓ Question




What is the DrugBank accession number of atorvastatin?
Search for the brand name Lipitor. Where do you land?







NoteShow answer






DB01076. Every DrugBank drug has a stable accession: DB + 5 digits.
On the same entry. DrugBank indexes brand names and synonyms, but the entry is always the active substance, not a commercial product.

title: One drug along the DrugBank page
text:
4 Reading the entry page


As in UniProt, the left-hand menu stays fixed as you scroll and shows what the entry holds. We will follow it from top to bottom:



Identification
Pharmacology
Interactions
Products
Categories
Chemical Identifiers
References




Clinical Trials
Pharmacoeconomics
Properties
Spectra
Targets, Enzymes
Carriers, Transporters



We will skip Clinical Trials, Pharmacoeconomics and Spectra today.

4.1 The summary card
At the top of the page is the “ID card” of the drug: structure, description, DrugBank ID, modality, number of indicated conditions, clinical trials by phase, therapeutic categories and mechanism of action.






Warning❓ Question




What is the modality of atorvastatin?
How many clinical trials are listed in Phase 4? Why is an approved drug still being tested?
In the Identification section, which Groups is atorvastatin in?







NoteShow answer






Small molecule (as opposed to, for example, an antibody).

Phase 4 trials take place after approval: they monitor long-term safety, compare treatments, or test new uses.

Approved and Investigational: it is marketed, and still under study.








4.2 Identification
Read the Background paragraph.






Warning❓ Question




When was atorvastatin first synthesised, and when was it approved by the FDA?
Unlike some other statins, atorvastatin does not need activation. What does that mean?







NoteShow answer






Synthesised in 1985, approved by the FDA in 1996.
It is given in its active form. Some statins (for example lovastatin and simvastatin) are prodrugs that must be converted in the body before they can inhibit the enzyme.








4.3 Pharmacology
This is the core of the entry. Read Mechanism of action and the small target table below it.






Warning❓ Question




Which enzyme does atorvastatin inhibit, and which reaction does that enzyme catalyse?
Atorvastatin blocks cholesterol synthesis in the liver. Why does that lower cholesterol in the blood?
The target table lists five proteins, each with a letter badge, A or U. Which one has an A, and what do you think the letters mean? (Hint: Look at the Targets cards at the bottom of the page and compare this table with its Pharmacological action field.)







NoteShow answer






Competitive inhibitor of HMG-CoA (3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A) reductase. It converts HMG-CoA to mevalonate, the rate-limiting step of cholesterol synthesis.
Liver cells with less cholesterol produce more LDL receptors, which pull LDL (sometimes called the “bad cholesterol”) out of the blood.
Only HMG-CoA reductase has an A: binding to it is known to cause the drug’s effect (Pharmacological Action: yes). The other four (DPP4, AHR, HDAC2, NR1I3) have U: the drug binds them, but whether that matters is Unknown.






Now read carefully in the Pharmacology section the fields related to pharmacokinetic characteristics of the drug:

Absorption,
Protein binding,
Metabolism,
Route of elimination and
Half-life.







Warning❓ Question




What is the absolute oral bioavailability, and why is it so low?
Which enzyme is mainly responsible for the metabolism? Are the metabolites active? (Look at the metabolite tree.)
The half-life of atorvastatin is 14 hours, yet the effect lasts longer. Why?
How is atorvastatin mainly eliminated?







NoteShow answer






14%, because of extensive first-pass metabolism in the gut wall and liver.
Cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4 gene), producing ortho- and para-hydroxylated metabolites. Yes, the metabolites are active: they account for about 70% of the circulating HMG-CoA reductase inhibition.
The active metabolites have half-lives of up to 30 hours.
In the bile. Less than 1% is eliminated by the kidneys.






Genes can change how a patient handles a drug. Re-read the end of the Absorption section, then scroll to the Pharmacogenomic Effects/ADRs table.






Warning❓ Question




Patients homozygous for the SLCO1B1 c.521T>C variant have a 2.45-fold higher atorvastatin AUC. SLCO1B1 gene encodes OATP1B1 protein, which carries the drug from the blood into liver cells. Why would these patients be at greater risk of muscle toxicity? (Hint: See the Myopathy/Rhabdomyolysis description in the Pharmacodynamics section.)
Which three genes are listed in the Pharmacogenomic Effects/ADRs table? Do they change the drug’s efficacy or its safety?







NoteShow answer






Less uptake into the liver means more drug stays in the blood and reaches muscle, where statins can cause myopathy (see Pharmacodynamics). The higher dose in the wrong tissue is the problem, not a stronger effect.
HMGCR and CYP3A4 (CYP3A4*1B)describe efficacy: a greater or smaller reduction in LDL cholesterol; while KIF6 describes a safety related finding (reduced risk of major cardiovascular event).












Warning❓ Question



Critical thinking question
Ask your favourite Large Language Model (LLM) AI chat:
“What is the half-life of atorvastatin, which enzyme metabolises it, and what is your source? Answer briefly.”
Compare the answer with DrugBank. Does it match? Does the source exist and say what the model claims? Which would you cite in a report, and why?






NoteShow answer





LLMs usually get well-known facts like these right, but they can mix up values (for example, the half-life of the drug and of its metabolites), and the references they give may be inaccurate or invented. DrugBank attaches a numbered reference to each statement, which you can open and check.







4.4 Interactions






Tip🔬 Hands on




In Drug Interactions, note the number of entries under the default APPROVED tab, then click ALL DRUGS.
Type clarithromycin in the table’s search box.
Read the Food Interactions.









Warning❓ Question




How many interactions with approved drugs are listed? Why does the number grow under ALL DRUGS?
What does DrugBank say about clarithromycin? Explain it using what you learnt in the Pharmacology section.
Can Atorvastatin be taken with food? Which food should patients avoid, and why?







NoteShow answer







ALL DRUGS () also includes investigational, experimental, nutraceutical and other substances.

“The risk or severity of rhabdomyolysis can be increased when Clarithromycin is combined with Atorvastatin.” This is because Clarithromycin decreases the metabolism of atorvastatin. It is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, so atorvastatin levels rise, and with them the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis.
Atorvastatin can be taken with or without food. Grapefruit should be avoided because it increases the risk of myopathy (since it inhibits CYP3A4 in the gut wall).








4.5 Products and Categories






Warning❓ Question




In Products, look at International/Other Brands. Under which brand name is atorvastatin sold in Portugal? By which pharmaceutical company?
How many generic prescription products are listed? Can you propose why so many?
Look at Unapproved/Other Products. Does anything surprise you? In which country are they sold?
In Categories, decode the ATC code C10AA05 level by level. The other ATC codes are combination products: with which kinds of drugs is atorvastatin combined?







NoteShow answer






Sortis is the brand name in Portugal, sold by Pfizer.
909 generics. Since the patent has expired, many companies sell generics, in several strengths and pack sizes.
Two oral liquids, including a “coffee”, list atorvastatin as an ingredient. A database faithfully records what has been registered somewhere, not only what makes medical sense. Always check the source.
C cardiovascular system › C10 lipid modifying agents › C10A lipid modifying agents, plain › C10AA HMG CoA reductase inhibitors › C10AA05 atorvastatin. The combinations add other cardiovascular drugs: ezetimibe (another lipid-lowering drug), antihypertensives (amlodipine, perindopril, ramipril, candesartan) and acetylsalicylic acid. Several of them are “polypills” for cardiovascular prevention.








4.6 Chemical Identifiers and Properties
The Chemical Identifiers section provides standardized names and machine-readable representations that uniquely identify a drug’s chemical structure and allow it to be linked across databases.








Identifier
What it is
Typical use




UNII
FDA Unique Ingredient Identifier
Standardized identification of substances in FDA-related data.


CAS Registry Number
A unique numeric identifier assigned by Chemical Abstracts Service
Searching and matching chemicals across regulatory and chemical databases.


InChIKey
Fixed 27-character hash derived from InChI
Compact, searchable identifier for web and database searches.


InChI
IUPAC International Chemical Identifier; a standardized structural text identifier
Precise structure-based database linking.


IUPAC name
Systematic chemical name following IUPAC rules
Unambiguous human-readable description of the molecule.


SMILES
Text string encoding the 2D molecular structure
Input for cheminformatics tools, structure drawing, and computational analysis.



SMILES and InChI describe the structure, while CAS, UNII, and DrugBank IDs are database identifiers used to retrieve and cross-reference the same compound. DrugBank also provides structure downloads in formats such as SDF, SMILES, and InChI for computational workflows.
The Properties lists experimental and predicted physicochemical values.
Note | A classic first check in drug design is Lipinski’s Rule of Five (Ro5): a rule of thumb in medicinal chemistry used to estimate whether a small molecule is likely to be orally bioavailable in humans (i.e., absorbed well enough after ingestion to reach its target). It was introduced by Christopher Lipinski in 1997 and is a screening guideline, not proof that a compound will be an effective drug.
According to this rule, an active drug usually has no more than one violation of these rules:








Property
Preferred limit
Why it matters




Molecular weight
≤ 500 Da
Very large molecules often have poor membrane permeability


Calculated log P (ClogP)
≤ 5
Measures lipophilicity; too high can reduce solubility and increase nonspecific binding


Hydrogen-bond donors
≤ 5
Mainly OH and NH groups; too many can impede passage through membranes


Hydrogen-bond acceptors
≤ 10
Mainly O and N atoms; excessive polarity can reduce permeability









Warning❓ Question




In the Properties section, sub-section Predicted Properties, what does DrugBank say about the Rule of Five? Using the molecular weight (shown in the Identification section), logP, donor and acceptor counts, which rules are broken?
You will find three different logP values on the Properties section. Why do they differ?
Atorvastatin fails the Rule of Five, yet it is one of the most used oral drugs. What does that tell you about such rules?







NoteShow answer






Rule of Five: No. Molecular weight 558.6 > 500, and logP 5.39 (Chemaxon) > 5. Donors (4) and Acceptors (5) are fine.
One is experimental (6.36) and two are predicted by different programs (ALOGPS 4.24, Chemaxon 5.39). Predictions depend on the method; always check which value you are using.
They are quick filters, not laws. Atorvastatin is well absorbed (the predicted ADMET table also says so); its low bioavailability comes from first-pass metabolism, which these rules do not capture.








4.7 Targets, Enzymes, Carriers and Transporters
The last part of the page has one card per protein associated with this drug (targets, metabolizing enzymes, carriers, and transporters), each with its UniProt ID, Pharmacological action and Actions (inhibitor, substrate, inducer, binder…).






Warning❓ Question




How many enzymes, carriers and transporters are listed? (Hint: Look at the left-hand menu.)
Which carrier is listed? How does it relate to the Protein binding percentage you read earlier in the Pharmacology section?
In the HMG-CoA reductase card, click the UniProt ID P04035. What is the UniProt entry name, and where is the protein located in the cell?







NoteShow answer






10 enzymes, 1 carrier, 10 transporters.
Albumin (action: binder). Since the carrier protein is albumin, the drug is transported in the blood bound to albumin, which explains why more than 98% of atorvastatin in plasma is protein-bound.
The protein name in UniProt is HMDH_HUMAN. It is a membrane protein located in the endoplasmic reticulum and in the peroxisome. Note that the DrugBank and UniProt databases are linked by the shared accession number P04035.

title: One drug along the DrugBank page
text:
5 From drug to structure
DrugBank tells you that atorvastatin binds HMG-CoA reductase. The Protein Data Bank (PDB) shows you how, atom by atom.






Tip🔬 Hands on




In DrugBank, copy the InChIKey of atorvastatin (Chemical Identifiers).
Go to References › External Links. Note the PDBe Ligand ID and click the entry under PDB Entries (1hwk).
You are now on the RCSB PDB page. Scroll to Small Molecules.









Warning❓ Question




Compare the InChIKey of the ligand with the one you copied (Hint: You can use CTRL + f to search for the InChIKey). What do you conclude?
Which experimental method was used, and at what resolution?
The protein in this structure has four chains. How many copies of atorvastatin are bound? (Hint: You can hide the Polymer and the Water in the right-hand side menu, and keep visible only the Ligands. If you hover the mouse over the ligands you can see their name in the bottom right corner (id 117)).







NoteShow answer






In the PDB entry 1HWK, ligand 117 has the same InChIKey (XUKUURHRXDUEBC-KAYWLYCHSA-N) as atorvastatin in the DrugBank entry, so ligand 117 in PDB is atorvastatin, even though the two databases use different identifiers for it.
X-ray diffraction, 2.22 Å (Istvan and Deisenhofer, Science, 2001).
Four, one in each chain.

text:
Key points






TipTake home messages




A DrugBank entry gathers chemistry, mechanism, pharmacokinetics, interactions and products of a drug in one place.
Targets explain the effect; enzymes and transporters explain most interactions and much of the variability between patients.
Not every listed target matters: check the pharmacological action.
Predictions (logP, Rule of Five, ADMET) are useful filters, not facts.
Shared identifiers (UniProt ID, InChIKey, PDB ID) connect drug, protein and structure databases.

title: ClinPGx | From genotype to prescription
section: 1 Why is ClinPGx relevant for pharmaceutical sciences?
text:
1 Why is ClinPGx relevant for pharmaceutical sciences?
Two patients receive the same drug at the same dose. One responds well, the other has no benefit, and a third may have a serious adverse reaction. Part of this variability is genetic. Pharmacogenomics (PGx) studies how inherited variation in our genes changes the way we respond to medicines.
In previous classes you followed one entity at a time: a gene in Ensembl, a protein in UniProt, a structure in PDB, a drug in DrugBank. ClinPGx sits on top of all of them and answers a clinical question:

“Given this patient’s genotype, should I change the drug or the dose?”

That is a question pharmacists will increasingly be asked to answer, which is why this is our final database.

3 Key concepts before we start
You only need six ideas to use ClinPGx well. Read them now; you will use each one during the session.






Note📘 Concept 1: Pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic genes




Pharmacokinetic (PK) genes change what the body does to the drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion. Most are enzymes (e.g. the cytochromes P450, CYP2C19, CYP2D6) or transporters (e.g. SLCO1B1).
Pharmacodynamic (PD) genes change what the drug does to the body: the target (e.g. VKORC1 for warfarin) or the immune response (e.g. HLA-B and severe skin reactions).









Note📘 Concept 2: Star alleles and haplotypes



A gene can carry several variants at once. The combination of variants found together on one copy of a chromosome is a haplotype. In pharmacogenes, haplotypes are named with star (*) alleles: CYP2C19*1, CYP2C19*2, CYP2C19*17, and so on.

*1 is usually the reference (normal) allele.
Each other star allele is defined by one or more core variants, often identified by their dbSNP rsID (e.g. rs4244285).
The official naming authority for star alleles is PharmVar.









Note📘 Concept 3: Diplotype



We have two copies of each autosomal gene (one from each parent). The pair of star alleles a person carries is their diplotype, written CYP2C19*1/*2. A diplotype is the PGx equivalent of a genotype.








Note📘 Concept 4: Allele function and phenotype



Each star allele is assigned a function: normal, decreased, no function, or increased function. Combining the two alleles of a diplotype predicts a phenotype. For drug-metabolising enzymes the phenotypes are:

How do two alleles give one phenotype? Think of each allele as contributing some enzyme activity, and add the two contributions together. For CYP2C19, the rules used by CPIC are:

Notice the last two rows: one no function allele is enough to reduce activity, even when the other allele has increased function. These rules are gene-specific, which is why each CPIC guideline has its own genotype-to-phenotype table.








Note📘 Concept 5: Prodrugs turn the logic upside down



For most drugs, a poor metabolizer clears the drug slowly, so drug levels rise and the risk of toxicity increases. But a prodrug is inactive until an enzyme converts it into the active form. For a prodrug, a poor metabolizer makes less active drug, so the risk is lack of efficacy.
Clopidogrel, our example today, is a prodrug activated mainly by CYP2C19.








Note📘 Concept 6: The ClinPGx knowledge pyramid



ClinPGx builds knowledge in layers, from raw literature to clinical action:





flowchart BT
  A["Published papers<br/>(PubMed)"] --> B["Variant annotations<br/>one finding from one paper"]
  B --> C["Summary annotations<br/>all findings for one variant-drug pair,<br/>graded with a level of evidence"]
  C --> D["Guidelines and drug labels<br/>CPIC, DPWG, FDA, EMA...<br/>what to do in the clinic"]


 From published papers to prescribing guidance. 



The higher you go, the more curated and the more clinically actionable the information becomes.


The whole lesson follows this chain:

Open https://www.clinpgx.org/.

Find the search bar, the CPIC section, and the link to the gene-drug pairs list.









Warning❓ Question




Which kinds of entities can you search for?
Open the gene-drug pairs list (https://www.clinpgx.org/pairs). What is it built from?







NoteShow answer






Genes, drugs (called chemicals), variants and haplotypes, diseases, as well as guidelines, labels, pathways and literature.
It lists gene-drug pairs that have been annotated in guidelines or drug labels from CPIC, DPWG (the Dutch Pharmacogenetics Working Group) and the FDA. It is a quick way to see which pairs are clinically relevant.

5 The gene page: CYP2C19
As in UniProt, the best way to find an entry is a unique identifier, here the official HGNC gene symbol.






Tip🔬 Hands on: open the CYP2C19 page




Type CYP2C19 in the search bar.
Select the gene result (not a drug or a variant).
Note the identifier in the URL. It starts with PA (e.g. PA124).
Browse the tabs of the gene page.



Every ClinPGx object has a stable PA identifier (a legacy of PharmGKB), in the same way that UniProt has accessions like P04000 and DrugBank has identifiers like DB00758.






Warning❓ Question




Is CYP2C19 a pharmacokinetic or a pharmacodynamic gene? Why?
CYP2C19 is labelled a VIP. What does that mean?
List three drugs (or drug classes) for which a CPIC guideline exists for CYP2C19.
In the cross-references, find the identifiers for Ensembl and UniProt. Do you recognise them from earlier classes?







NoteShow answer






Pharmacokinetic: CYP2C19 is a liver enzyme that metabolises drugs.
Very Important Pharmacogene: a gene with strong, well documented pharmacogenomic relevance, for which ClinPGx curators write a dedicated summary.
Among others: clopidogrel, proton pump inhibitors (e.g. omeprazole, pantoprazole), voriconazole, some antidepressants (e.g. citalopram, escitalopram, sertraline) and tricyclic antidepressants.
Ensembl ENSG00000165841 (chromosome 10) and UniProt P33261 (CP2CJ_HUMAN). The same gene and protein you could have studied in previous classes, now viewed from the clinical side.












Tip🔗 Connection: UniProt and PDB



Open the UniProt entry P33261 in a new tab and check the Function and Subcellular location sections. Then go to the Structure section, or search PDB for 4GQS, a crystal structure of human CYP2C19.
You now know where the enzyme is (endoplasmic reticulum membrane of liver cells) and what it looks like (a heme-containing P450 fold). ClinPGx tells you what happens to patients when its gene varies.
